slides.notes: So, when a file is stored on disk, the OS must maintain a record of where its blocks are located. The directory entry points to this record, while the allocation method determines how those block locations are organised. This organisation impacts access speed, fragmentation, and how easily the file can grow. We’ll look at three classic approaches: contiguous, linked, and indexed allocation.

slides.notes: The main advantage of contiguous allocation is that all file blocks are next to each other. This makes both sequential and direct access fast. For direct access, the OS can calculate the required block using start + block number. However, there is a problem when files are created and deleted: small free spaces can appear between files, causing external fragmentation.Also, if a file needs to grow, there may not be enough free blocks immediately after it, so the file may need to be moved.

Linked allocation scatters a file's blocks anywhere on disk, chaining them with a pointer to the next block stored inside each block.

slides.title: Linked Allocation
slides.body:
Chained Block Pointers
Directory stores only a pointer to the first block
01
02

No external fragmentation — any free block is usable

slides.notes:
In linked allocation, the directory needs to remember only the first block of the file. 
From that block, the OS follows the pointers to find the remaining blocks. 
Because the file can use free blocks from different locations, the blocks do not need to be next to each other, so external fragmentation is avoided. 
If the file grows, the OS can simply find another free block and link it to the end of the chain.

slides.body:

slides.notes:
Linked allocation is useful for flexible file storage, but accessing a specific block can be slower. 
For example, to reach the 5th block, the OS may need to follow the chain from the first block through the earlier blocks. 
Each block also uses some space to store its pointer. If a pointer is damaged, the OS may lose the link to the following blocks, making that part of the file inaccessible.

Indexed allocation can place a file’s data blocks in different free locations, so it avoids external fragmentation. 
The limitation is the size of the index block.
 If a file has more data blocks than the index block can hold addresses for, the OS needs additional levels or combined index structures to store more addresses. 
Also, the index block uses disk space even though it does not store the file’s actual data.

slides.title: Two Tracking Approaches
slides.body:
FAT And Inode
These two common structures used by file systems to track the disk blocks belonging to files
File Allocation Table
inode
slides.notes:
After looking at the three allocation methods, let’s see how file systems actually keep track of file blocks.
 Two common approaches are FAT and inodes.
They both help the file system locate a file’s data on disk, 
but they store and organize the block information differently. We’ll look at each approach and see how it works.

slides.title: FAT Table Mechanism
slides.body:
Cluster Chain Links
The File Allocation Table sits near the start of the disk with one entry per cluster, chaining a file's clusters together
0
1

slides.notes:
Now, let’s understand how the File Allocation Table, or FAT, tracks file storage. FAT is maintained near the start of the disk, and it contains one entry for each cluster. These entries are used to connect the clusters belonging to a file, forming a chain. 
In the diagram, the FAT contains entries for Cluster A, Cluster B, and Cluster C, while the disk blocks are shown separately as the actual storage locations. The FAT acts like a map that tells the OS which cluster belongs to the file and which cluster should be accessed next. So, instead of searching the entire disk, the OS can follow these links to locate the file’s data

slides.title: FAT Table Mechanism
slides.body:
Cluster Chain Links
Directory entry stores only the file's starting cluster number
01
02
03
Each FAT entry holds the number of the next cluster
A special end-of-file marker closes the chain
slides.notes: Let’s see how the FAT chain is followed. The directory first gives the OS the starting cluster of the file. The OS checks that cluster’s FAT entry to find the next cluster, then repeats this process for each cluster. For example, if the chain is 5 → 9 → 16, the FAT entries tell the OS to move from cluster 5 to 9, and then from 9 to 16. When the OS reaches the end-of-file marker, it knows that the file has no more clusters.

slides.title: FAT Table Mechanism
slides.body:
Cluster Chain Links
Entry value 0 marks a cluster as free
04
05
06
A bad-cluster marker flags a damaged cluster
Two FAT copies are kept on disk for redundancy
slides.notes: FAT entries can also show whether a cluster is available or unusable. A zero value indicates a free cluster that can be allocated to a file, while a bad-cluster marker identifies a cluster that should not be used. FAT-based file systems also keep two copies of the FAT to provide redundancy if one copy is damaged or corrupted.

slides.title: FAT Chain Example
slides.body:
Tracing Cluster Links
File F starts at cluster 9, following the FAT entries reveals its full cluster chain and where it ends
slides.notes: Now, let’s trace a complete FAT chain using this example. File F starts at cluster 9, so we first check the FAT entry for cluster 9, which points to cluster 16. From 16, the entry points to 2, and cluster 2 then points to 22. Finally, the entry for cluster 22 contains EOF, meaning the chain has ended. So, the complete cluster chain for File F is 9 → 16 → 2 → 22 → EOF. This shows how FAT entries allow the OS to trace the file’s clusters one by one

slides.title: Inode Structure Basics
slides.body:
Metadata Plus Pointers
An inode is a fixed-size on-disk record holding a file's metadata and the pointers to its data clusters, identified by an inode number
Inode Record
1
2
3
File's metadata
Pointers
Inode Number
slides.notes: Now, let’s look at the inode, which provides a different way of tracking a file. An inode is a fixed-size on-disk record associated with a file and identified by an inode number. It stores the file’s metadata, such as information about the file, along with pointers that help locate its data clusters. In the diagram, the inode record contains entries such as 1, 2, and 3, with each inode number identifying a particular record. The selected inode then connects to the file’s metadata and its pointers, allowing the OS to obtain both information about the file and the locations of its data.

slides.title: Inode Structure Basics
slides.body:
Metadata Plus Pointers
Stores file type, permissions, owner and group IDs
01
02
03
Stores size, timestamps and a link count
Stores pointers to data clusters, not the file name
04
05
Directory entry maps a file name to an inode number
Multiple directory entries can point to one inode
slides.notes:
An inode stores the important information the file system needs to manage a file. 
This includes the file type, permissions, owner and group IDs, file size, timestamps, and link count. 
It also contains pointers to the file’s data blocks, but not the file name. The directory keeps the file name and maps it to the inode number. 
Because of this separation, multiple directory entries can point to the same inode and give the same file multiple names.

slides.title: Direct Indirect Pointers
slides.body:
Scaling File Size
A fixed-size inode cannot list pointers for a huge file directly, so it layers direct and indirect pointers to reach far more data blocks
slides.notes: Next, the challenge is that an inode has limited space, so storing the address of every data block would not work for very large files. To solve this, the inode uses a combination of direct and indirect pointers. Direct pointers can reach data blocks immediately, while indirect pointers lead to additional blocks that contain more addresses. This layered approach lets the same fixed-size inode handle files that are much larger than it could point to directly

slides.title: Direct Indirect Pointers
slides.body:
Scaling File Size
Direct pointers point straight to a data block
01
02
03
Single-indirect pointer leads to a block full of pointers
Double-indirect pointer leads to a block of single-indirect clusters
04
05
Triple-indirect pointer adds one more level of indirection
Each added level multiplies addressable file size sharply
slides.notes: Next, these pointers provide different levels of reach from the inode. A direct pointer gives the OS the address of a data block immediately. When more storage is needed, a single-indirect pointer takes us to another block that contains multiple data-block addresses. A double-indirect pointer adds another layer, pointing to blocks that themselves contain these address blocks. Triple-indirect pointer adds one more level. So, with every additional level, the number of data blocks that can be reached grows dramatically, allowing the inode to support very large files

slides.title: Free Space Management
slides.body: Free Space Management
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Free Space Management

slides.title: Free Space Tracking
slides.body:
Why It Matters?
Before allocating a new block, the operating system must quickly know which disk blocks are free, free space management maintains this record
Free Space Management In OS
Bitmap
Linked List
 Counting
Grouping
slides.notes:
Before the OS can give a new block to a file, it needs a quick way to find available space. 
This is called free space management. Different methods organize this information in different ways.
 A bitmap uses bits to represent block status, while a linked list connects free blocks. 
Counting records a starting block and how many consecutive blocks are free.
 Grouping keeps several free-block addresses together and uses one entry to point to another group.

slides.title: Free Space Tracking
slides.body:
Why It Matters?
Every deleted or new file changes free block status
01
02
Slow free-block lookup delays every file creation
slides.notes: Free space changes whenever files are created or deleted. When a file is deleted, its blocks become available for reuse. When a new file is created, the OS must find suitable free blocks for it. If finding those blocks takes too long, file creation and other file operations can become slower.

slides.title: Bitmap Method
slides.body:
One Bit Per Block
A bit vector reserves one bit per disk block, set to 1 for free and 0 for allocated, giving a compact free-space map

slides.notes:
The bitmap gives the OS a simple way to check block availability. Each disk block has one corresponding bit. 
For example, Block 1 has value 1, so the OS knows it is free, while Block 2 has value 0, so it is already in use.
 The OS can scan these bits to find free blocks and allocate them when needed. 
Because only one bit is used per block, the bitmap provides a compact way to track free space.

slides.body:
One Bit Per Block

slides.notes: The bitmap uses one bit for each disk block. So, if there are N blocks, the bitmap needs N bits, or N/8 bytes, because 8 bits make one byte. To find free space, the OS can scan the bitmap for a set bit, which represents a free block. It can also check multiple bits at once to skip fully allocated regions and find free blocks more quickly. This makes the bitmap simple and useful for finding consecutive free blocks.

slides.notes: Next, the Free List Method manages available disk space by connecting all the free blocks into a chain. Each free block contains a pointer to the next free block, so the OS can move through the list whenever it needs to find available space. In the diagram, the blocks marked 1 are free, while those marked 0 are allocated. The arrows show how the free blocks are linked together—for example, the OS can follow the pointers from one free block to the next instead of scanning the entire disk.

slides.body:
Chained Free Blocks
Operating system keeps only a pointer to the first free block
01

slides.notes: Now, think of the available disk blocks as a chain that the OS can maintain without keeping a separate record of every free block. The OS starts with the first free block, and from there each block tells it where to find the next one. When a block is needed for a new file, the OS removes it from this chain and moves the head pointer to the next available block. When a previously used block becomes free, it can be connected back into the chain. Since the information is maintained through the blocks themselves, this avoids the additional storage required by a bit vector. The limitation is that if the OS needs to locate a particular free block deeper in the list, it has to follow the chain sequentially.

Grouping stores the addresses of several free blocks inside the first free block, instead of chaining one pointer at a time

slides.notes: Next, the Grouping Method improves on the basic free-list approach by keeping several free-block addresses together instead of maintaining a separate link for every block. In the diagram, Block 1 is free, and it stores the addresses A1, A5, A6, and A8, which identify other available blocks. When the OS needs free space, it can obtain several available addresses from this group at once. This reduces the amount of sequential traversal needed compared with a simple linked list, especially when many free blocks need to be managed.

slides.title: Grouping Method
slides.body:
Batching Free Addresses
First free block holds addresses of the next n-1 free blocks
01
02
03
Last stored address points onward to another such group
Retrieves many free blocks in a single disk read
04
Cuts the number of pointer-following steps versus a plain linked list
slides.notes: Grouping manages free blocks in batches. The first free block stores the addresses of several other free blocks, and the last address can lead to the next group. For example, instead of following a separate link for every free block, the OS can obtain several free-block addresses from one group. This reduces the number of pointer-following steps and makes managing large amounts of free space more efficient than a simple linked list.

slides.title: Counting Method
slides.body:
Free Block Run
Counting exploits the fact that several consecutive blocks are often free together, storing a start address plus a count of contiguous free blocks
slides.notes: The Counting Method is useful when free blocks appear in consecutive runs. For example, if blocks 20 through 24 are free, the OS can record just the starting block 20 and a count of 5, instead of recording each block separately. This makes the free-space information more compact and helps the OS quickly identify a continuous region of free blocks.

slides.title: Counting Method
slides.body:
Free Block Run
Each free-list entry holds a first block address and a run length
01
02
03
One entry can represent many contiguous free blocks
Far fewer entries needed when free space is not scattered
04
Less efficient when free blocks are mostly isolated singles
slides.notes: So, the Counting Method represents free space in terms of continuous runs rather than individual blocks. Each entry records where the run begins and its run length, allowing one entry to describe several contiguous free blocks. This keeps the free-space record small when available blocks occur together. However, when free space becomes highly scattered and consists mostly of isolated blocks, the method needs many separate entries and becomes less efficient.

slides.title: File System Types
slides.body: File System Types
slides.notes: Now , we will be learning about the File System Types

slides.title: Why FS Types Differ
slides.body:
Allocation Meets Reality
A file system implements allocation, FAT/inode structures and free-space management into one deployable package, tuned to a device and OS
slides.notes: A real file system combines several mechanisms to manage files. It uses an allocation method to organize file data, a structure such as a FAT or inode to track that data and its metadata, and a free-space method to find available blocks. These mechanisms work together, and the exact design depends on the file system and the operating system or device where it is used.

slides.title: Why FS Types Differ
slides.body:
Allocation Meets Reality
FAT16, FAT32 target simple flash/removable media
01
02
03
NTFS targets Windows desktop and server volumes
ext2, ext3, ext4 target Linux systems
04
05
HFS+ / APFS target macOS and Apple devices
Journaling capability separates crash-safe from unsafe designs
slides.notes: Different file systems are designed for different operating systems, devices, and requirements. FAT16 and FAT32 are simple designs commonly associated with removable storage. NTFS provides features for Windows desktop and server systems, while ext2, ext3, and ext4 are widely used in Linux. HFS+ and APFS are associated with Apple systems, with APFS being the newer design. Some file systems also support journaling, which helps reduce the risk of file-system inconsistency after a crash by recording changes before they are fully applied.

slides.title: FAT16 vs FAT32
slides.body:
Cluster And Size Limits
FAT32 extends FAT16 by widening cluster addressing, removing FAT16's small-volume ceiling and raising maximum file and volume size.
slides.notes:
FAT32 was introduced to overcome several size limitations of FAT16. 
It uses 32-bit cluster numbers, with 28 bits actually used for cluster addressing, allowing many more clusters to be addressed. 
FAT16 has a fixed-size root directory, while FAT32 stores the root directory in the data area so it can grow. 
Both support large removable-storage volumes compared with older FAT variants, but FAT32 still has a maximum file size of 4 GB minus 1 byte. 
Neither FAT16 nor FAT32 provides journaling, so they do not record file-system changes in a journal for crash recovery.
tables: ~2 TB theoretical, 32 GB typical OS format
Dynamic, stored as a regular file

slides.title: FAT16 vs FAT32
slides.body:
FAT16 mostly obsolete, used only in legacy embedded devices
FAT32 still common on USB drives and SD cards
Cluster And Size Limits
FAT
slides.notes: FAT evolved from FAT12 to FAT16 and then FAT32 as storage requirements increased. FAT16 is now mostly found in older or legacy systems, while FAT32 remains common on removable storage such as USB drives and SD cards. FAT32 can support much larger volumes than FAT16 because it uses a wider cluster address space. The 2 TB figure should be presented as a commonly supported maximum rather than a universal theoretical limit, because actual limits depend on implementation and formatting choices.

slides.title: NTFS Overview
slides.body:
Windows Native File System
NTFS (New Technology File System) is Microsoft's modern file system, adding 
 Large-volume support absent in FAT
Journaling
Security
Large-volume support
slides.notes: NTFS is the modern file system commonly used by Windows. It provides journaling, which helps maintain file-system consistency after an unexpected shutdown. It also provides security features, such as permissions that control who can access files and folders. NTFS supports much larger storage volumes and files than the older FAT file systems, making it better suited for modern Windows computers and servers.

slides.notes: NTFS combines several features to make file management more reliable and secure. Journaling helps the file system recover metadata consistently after a crash. ACLs control which users or groups can access individual files and folders. NTFS also supports compression and transparent encryption. Instead of a simple FAT-style table, it uses the Master File Table (MFT) to maintain records about files and folders. These features allow NTFS to support much larger storage than FAT32.

slides.title: NTFS Overview
slides.body:
Windows Native File System
NTFS
slides.notes: NTFS was introduced by Microsoft in 1993 and provides several features beyond basic file storage. Journaling helps the file system recover more reliably after failures, while file compression can reduce the amount of storage needed. Transactions help maintain consistency when multiple related changes are made, and security features control access to files and folders. Together, these features make NTFS suitable for managing data on Windows systems.

slides.title: ext2 Filesystem
slides.body:
No Journaling Design
Uses inode structure with direct/indirect block pointers
01
02
03
Organises disk into block groups for locality
No journal — crash requires full fsck scan
04
05
Still used on flash media needing low write overhead
Superseded by ext3/ext4 for most modern Linux use
slides.notes: ext2 uses inodes and direct/indirect pointers to locate file data. It also divides the disk into block groups, keeping related data and metadata closer together for better locality. Unlike ext3 and ext4, ext2 has no journal, so after an unexpected shutdown, the file system may need a full fsck check to find and repair inconsistencies. The lack of journaling reduces write overhead, which can make ext2 useful in some environments, although it is largely replaced by ext3 and ext4 on modern Linux systems.

slides.title: Journaling Concept
slides.body:
Write Ahead Logging
Journaling writes an intended change to a dedicated log before modifying the real file system, so an interrupted operation can be completed or undone safely
Avoids full-disk consistency scan after unexpected shutdown
slides.notes: journaling keeps a record of important file-system changes before those changes are fully applied. If the system crashes during an update, the file system can use the journal during recovery to determine what changes need to be completed or restored to a consistent state. This greatly reduces the need for a lengthy full-file-system consistency check after an unexpected shutdown.

slides.title: Journaling Modes
slides.body:
Metadata Versus Full Data
File systems offer journaling modes trading recovery safety for speed, from journaling only metadata to journaling both metadata and file data
slides.notes: Moving on, journaling modes differ in how much information the file system records before making a change. A metadata-only approach protects the file system’s structure and bookkeeping while keeping write overhead lower. A full-data approach also records the actual file data, providing stronger protection if a crash happens during a write, but it requires more disk activity. So, the choice is essentially a trade-off between recovery safety and speed
tables: Metadata only, no data ordering guarantee

slides.title: Journaling Modes
slides.body:
Crash mid-write: journal shows update was logged, not confirmed
01
02
03
Remount replays the logged step, discarding the incomplete step
Filesystem returns to last consistent state within seconds
Metadata Versus Full Data
slides.notes: When a crash happens during a write, the journal helps the file system determine what was in progress. The journal shows that an update was recorded but not fully completed. During remount, the file system replays the logged operation or discards the incomplete operation as needed. This allows the file system to quickly return to a consistent state without checking the entire disk.

slides.title: ext3 Filesystem (third extended file system)
slides.body:
Journaling Added
Backward compatible with existing ext2 volumes
01
02
03
Journal records pending changes before they are applied
Recovery replays journal instead of scanning entire disk
04
05
Supports three journaling modes with different safety and speed
Still uses ext2's original block/inode layout otherwise
slides.notes: Moving on, ext3 builds on the existing ext2 design by introducing journaling, so the core block and inode structure remains familiar. Before making important file-system changes, the journal records what needs to be done. If a crash occurs, the system can use that record during recovery instead of checking the entire disk from scratch. ext3 also provides three journaling modes, allowing the system to balance recovery safety against performance. Because it remains backward compatible with ext2, the transition could be made without redesigning the entire file-system structure.

slides.title: ext4 Filesystem (fourth extended file system)
slides.body:
Extents Replace Pointers
Extents map a contiguous block range in one entry
01
02
03
Fewer metadata entries needed versus per-block pointers
Supports far larger file and volume sizes than ext3
04
05
Faster fsck, delayed allocation, and checksummed journal
Current default file system on most Linux distributions
slides.notes: Next, ext4 improves the way large files are represented by using extents instead of maintaining separate pointers for individual blocks. An extent can describe an entire contiguous range with a single entry, which reduces the amount of metadata the system has to manage. This allows ext4 to scale to much larger file and volume sizes than ext3. It also improves overall file-system operation through features such as faster fsck, delayed allocation, and a checksummed journal, making ext4 a more scalable and reliable choice for modern Linux systems.

slides.body:
macOS Native Filesystem
Uses a B-tree "catalog file" to index all files and folders for fast lookup

slides.notes: Moving on, HFS+ was designed as a native file system for macOS, with a focus on efficiently organizing and locating files. Its B-tree catalog file works like an index, allowing the system to quickly search through the large collection of files and folders instead of checking them one by one. Journaling helps preserve file-system consistency after a crash, while support for Unicode file names, hard and symbolic links, and large volumes provides flexibility for everyday macOS storage needs.

macOS Native Filesystem
APFS (2017) superseded it, adding copy-on-write, snapshots and SSD/flash optimization

Still seen on older Macs and mechanical/Time Machine drives

slides.notes: Next, HFS+ was eventually replaced by APFS in 2017, as storage technology and macOS requirements evolved. APFS introduced features such as copy-on-write and snapshots, along with optimizations designed for SSD/flash storage. HFS+ hasn’t disappeared completely, though; it can still be encountered on older Macs and some mechanical or Time Machine drives. So, HFS+ is mainly important today for understanding older macOS storage systems
